implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy supports concrete table inheritance explicitly: mark each subclass's mapper with __mapper_args__ = {'concrete': True} - or derive the base from AbstractConcreteBase, which does it for you - and every class maps to its own table containing its own plus its inherited columns, with no table needed for an abstract base. For polymorphic reads SQLAlchemy builds a UNION ALL of all concrete tables through polymorphic_union(), NULL-padding the columns that do not apply and synthesizing the type tag; the documentation warns that concrete inheritance 'presents more configurational challenges' than single or joined inheritance and restricts relationships that target the concrete base. Use it when leaf-scoped queries dominate and per-table freedom matters; use joined table inheritance when base-typed queries and relationships are the norm.
pitfalls: polymorphic_identity is not persisted under concrete inheritance - SQLAlchemy synthesizes the discriminator inside the union query, so a raw SQL read of one table cannot tell you the type.
Relationships to the concrete base are limited: a foreign key to 'any Employee' has no table to point at, and the documentation restricts relationship configuration accordingly.
The union pads non-applicable columns with NULL and needs compatible column types across subclasses, so a type change in one table silently changes the union's shape.

variants.name: Django abstract base model with one model per concrete type
variants.idiom_name: Meta.abstract = True base model plus one model/table per concrete type
variants.implementation_notes: Django has no concrete inheritance mapping: an abstract base model (class Meta: abstract = True) contributes its fields to every concrete model, and each concrete model gets its own table with those fields copied - the documented Django way to share columns without a join. Mixed collections must be assembled in Python from separate querysets or with a raw UNION query, because Django's other inheritance features point elsewhere (multi-table inheritance joins a parent table, proxy models share one table). Choose this when you want Django's ORM and per-table storage and accept that hierarchy-wide reads are not one query.
variants.code_sketch:
class Employee(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=64)

    class Meta:
        abstract = True

class Engineer(Employee):      # table app_engineer: id, name, salary
    salary = models.FloatField()

class Manager(Employee):       # table app_manager: id, name, department
    department = models.CharField(max_length=64)
pitfalls: Abstract base fields are copied per model: renaming or retyping a shared field is a migration on every concrete table, and Django will not warn about drift.
There is no polymorphic queryset - Engineer.objects and Manager.objects are separate - so a mixed, paginated list needs a raw UNION query with NULL padding.
Each table has its own auto-increment pk, so ids are not unique across the hierarchy and anything referencing 'any employee' by id is ambiguous.
